summary: Renan worked in religious studies, history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Paris seminaries, Collège de France, and under Eugène Burnouf and Etienne Marc Quatremère. He held posts at the Bibliothèque nationale de France and as professor and administrator at Collège de France.

Sosa is a philosopher who earned degrees at the University of Miami and University of Pittsburgh, studying under Roderick M. Chisholm. He served as a professor at Brown University from 1964 and as Board of Governors Professor at Rutgers University (1998–2006).

Curtius was a scholar of history and archaeology who studied at Bonn, Göttingen, and Berlin under Welcker, Karl Otfried Müller, and August Boeckh. He held professorships at Berlin and Göttingen (1855–1867) and directed the Altes Museum (c. 1872–1896).

Förstemann worked in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at Berlin and Halle under August Friedrich Pott, Karl Lachmann, and Franz Bopp. He served as librarian at the Fürstlich Stolberg-Wernigerödische Bibliothek and headed the Dresden library from 1865 to 1887.

Fürlinger works in religious studies and Indology, completing his habilitation at the University of Vienna. His career includes posts at St. Virgil Salzburg (1991–2001), University of Vienna (2006–2016), and multiple leadership and research roles at the University for Continuing Education Krems.

Haas specialized in Indology, studying at Bonn, Tübingen, and Berlin, where he studied under Albrecht Weber. He held posts at the British Museum from 1866 and served as Professor of Sanskrit at University College London from 1875.

Eitel was a scholar in Sinology and Buddhist studies. He studied at Blaubeuren and Maulbronn seminaries and earned his MA and PhD at the University of Tübingen. He served as professor and lecturer in German at the University of Adelaide (c. 1897–1908).

Kuhn worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Berlin, Tübingen, and Halle under Albrecht Weber and Rudolf von Roth. He held professorships at Heidelberg (1875) and Munich (1877–1917).

Leumann was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Zurich, Geneva, Berlin, Strasbourg, and Leipzig, under teachers including Albrecht Weber. He held posts at Oxford, served as professor and rector at Strasbourg, and later became honorary professor at Freiburg (1919).

Arndt was a German historian who studied at the universities of Greifswald and Jena. He held academic posts at the University of Greifswald from c. 1800 to 1811 and at the University of Bonn from c. 1818 to 1860.

Osiander worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the Maulbronn and Blaubeuren seminaries and the University of Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth, earning a Dr. phil. He later served as Repetent at Maulbronn/Blaubeuren (c. 1856–1858) and Tübinger Stift (1857–1860).

Steinkellner specializes in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, having studied under Erich Frauwallner. He served as director at the University of Vienna (1973–2006) and director of the Austrian Academy of Sciences' Institute for Cultural and Intellectual History of Asia (c. 1991–2006).

Trumpp worked in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at the Tübinger Stift and under Rudolf von Roth, held an assistantship at the East India Company, and was a Privatdozent at Tübingen before becoming professor at the University of Munich in 1874.

Waldschmidt was an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Paul Deussen, Emil Sieg, Heinrich Lüders, August Hermann Francke, and Albert Grünwedel. He served at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin and as chair of Indology at the University of Göttingen (1936–1965).

Windisch specialized in Indology and linguistics, studying at the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius, Friedrich Ritschl, Friedrich Zarncke, and Hermann Brockhaus. He held chairs of comparative linguistics at Heidelberg (1872) and Strasbourg (1875), and was long affiliated with Leipzig.
Zinn was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He held academic posts at the University of Hamburg (c. 1947–1951), Saarland University (1951–1956), and the University of Tübingen (c. 1951–1978).

Rousselle worked in Sinology and Buddhist studies, studying at Munich, Freiburg, Berlin, and Heidelberg. He held posts at Peking University (1924–1929), directed the Sino-Indian Institute, taught at Frankfurt from 1935, and directed the China-Institut Frankfurt beginning in 1931.
Andreasen is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Japanology, and religious studies. He studied at the University of Copenhagen and served as a visiting researcher at Otani University in 1992.

Nishimura is a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. He studied at Hanazono University, under Zenkei Shibayama, and at Kyoto University (PhD). He served as president, vice president, and director at Hanazono University, and directed the Institute for Zen Studies (c. 1989–2005).
Kawasaki is a scholar of Buddhist studies. Records attest him as director of the Buddhist Cultural Institute in 1999 and as president of Kyushu Ryukoku Gakkai in 2002.
